I'm looking for creative, motivated teammates skilled in programming, CAD, electronics, or hardware design who enjoy turning ambitious ideas into reality!
summary: Daily Orbit is a one-minute daily health check for astronauts on long missions, where a doctor is far away. The astronaut looks at their webcam, which reads their pulse and how often they blink. Two quick vision tests check each eye, and a few taps record sleep, mood and symptoms. The app compares every reading with that astronaut’s own usual numbers, not an average person’s, and marks each one green, yellow or red. It then gives one daily answer: Go, Go with limits, or No-go. If something looks wrong, it first checks whether it is just that person, the whole crew, or a broken sensor. If someone needs help, it shows who to tell, in order: themselves, a crewmate, the crew medical officer, then the flight surgeon on Earth. We built it from NASA bed-rest, solar-storm and planet-position data, and every explanation cites one of 87 sources. We tested it on a real NASA bed-rest participant, and it flagged their weight loss as red on 12 of 18 days, compared with 3 days using our first rules. This is a prototype, not a medical device.
details:
What it does and who it helps. On a long mission, the nearest doctor can be minutes of light time away, and on Mars up to 22 minutes each way. Daily Orbit gives each crew member a one-minute check and tells them what to do next. The webcam reads pulse and blinking. Two vision tests check each eye. A few taps record sleep, mood and symptoms. If the light or framing is bad, it asks for a retake instead of guessing. Logging covers blood pressure, temperature, blood sugar, body mass, food and water, a reaction test and body checks, 28 indicators in all. These include the six the brief names: blood pressure, heart rate, blood sugar, body temperature, sleep hours and mood.

How it decides. Each reading is compared with that person’s own history and shown green, yellow (Watch), red (Act), or gray (not enough good data). There are no clinical thresholds. Today makes one Go, Go with limits, or No-go call and shows the checks behind it. Related readings that drift together raise a pattern with a care plan. Before anyone escalates, each alert checks whether the change is the person’s own, shared by the whole crew (air, food, schedule), or a faulty sensor, so a broken blood-pressure cuff never climbs the ladder. Ask Orbit “What should I do?” walks the four-step ladder: self-care, crewmate, crew medical officer, flight surgeon. If the medical officer is the one who is sick, a backup takes over. The crew member chooses what is sent to Earth.

The intended impact. A crew member keeps their own health picture without waiting for the ground. Medical staff get early, comparable flags instead of a bad day found late. Points reward showing up, never a health value, so nobody has a reason to hide a bad day.

How NASA data makes it possible

  • NASA bed-rest case report forms (Life Sciences Data Archive) give Crew 3’s 30-day history. Replaying one participant day by day, our rules held their real weight loss at Act on 12 of 18 days (the old rules: 3), with no extra false alarms. It’s one person on a ground analog, a sanity check and not clinical validation.
  • NASA DONKI solar particle events (494 events, 6 replayable), LRO CRaTER dose rates and GOES proton flux power a solar-storm replay and the shelter alert. A mission forecast shows bone loss and career radiation to the end of the mission.
  • JPL planet positions give today’s real Earth-Mars distance and light time, and the next solar-conjunction blackout.
  • NASA HRP risks, Spaceflight Standard Measures and NASA-STD-3001 briefs tie every indicator to a NASA risk. 87 sources (63 NASA) back every explanation and escalation step, and each page shows which sources it rests on.

How we built it. React 19, TypeScript, Vite, Dexie (IndexedDB) and MediaPipe Face Landmarker. It runs in the browser with nothing to install. Camera frames are processed on the device and discarded, all data stays on the device, and the app makes no network calls while it runs. 449 automated tests.

Why it’s different. It treats the person as their own control: no population thresholds, no points for good numbers. It checks whether a change is the person’s, the crew’s or the sensor’s before anyone is alarmed. It adapts to the mission: ISS, lunar surface, lunar rover, Mars transit and Mars base, with real Mars light time. Judges can press J to run a one-click story, such as a fever, a CO2 build-up, a faulty cuff or a real solar storm.

Limits. This is a prototype, not a medical device. Webcam heart rate is not clinically validated, and the vision tests are self-checks, not eye exams. The radiation dose is a labeled simulation with no shielding model. Crews 1 and 2 are simulated and labeled on screen.
